title: Centralizer of the regular representation, over an arbitrary group
content: The module docstring poses the open question from the cayleys-theorem chain: Cayley embeds G into Equiv.Perm G as the left-regular representation L g : x ↦ g·x; identify the centralizer of L(G) inside the full symmetric group and pin down when the left- and right-regular representations coincide. Working over an arbitrary group G (no finiteness, strictly more general than the parent's Fin n setting), the answer is that the centralizer of L(G) is the right-regular image R(G), and the two coincide iff G is abelian — the centralizer half of the holomorph picture.
mathContext: $L(G), R(G) \le \operatorname{Sym}(G)$; goal: $C_{\operatorname{Sym}(G)}(L(G)) = R(G)$ and $L(G)=R(G)\iff G$ abelian.

title: The two regular representations as homomorphisms — and why rightReg needs an inverse
content: leftReg G : G →* Equiv.Perm G is Equiv.mulLeft (x ↦ g·x); it is a homomorphism on the nose because Equiv.mulLeft (a·b) = Equiv.mulLeft a * Equiv.mulLeft b. rightReg G sends g ↦ Equiv.mulRight g⁻¹ (x ↦ x·g⁻¹). The inverse on the argument is forced: plain right multiplication is an ANTI-homomorphism (mulRight (a·b) = mulRight b * mulRight a), and combining mul_inv_rev with mulRight_mul repairs the order so rightReg is a genuine homomorphism. The apply lemmas leftReg_apply/rightReg_apply expose the underlying functions by rfl.
mathContext: $L(g): x \mapsto gx$ (a homomorphism), $\;R(g): x \mapsto xg^{-1}$ (the inverse converts the anti-homomorphism $x\mapsto xg$ into a homomorphism).

title: Both representations are faithful
content: leftReg_injective and rightReg_injective show the regular representations are injective, by the evaluate-at-1 device: from leftReg a = leftReg b, evaluating at 1 and using mul_one gives a = b; for rightReg, evaluating at 1 and using one_mul gives a⁻¹ = b⁻¹, then inv_injective. Faithfulness is what makes the abelian characterisation an honest statement about G rather than about its image in the symmetric group.
mathContext: $L, R$ injective: $\;L(a)=L(b)\Rightarrow a\cdot 1 = b\cdot 1$; $\;R(a)=R(b)\Rightarrow 1\cdot a^{-1}=1\cdot b^{-1}$.

title: Centralizer of the left-regular image is the right-regular image
content: centralizer_leftReg_range is the headline: Subgroup.centralizer ↑(leftReg G).range = (rightReg G).range. Forward inclusion is the classical evaluate-at-1 rigidity — if σ commutes with every left translation, evaluating the commutativity equation (leftReg x)·σ = σ·(leftReg x) at the point 1 (via DFunLike.congr_fun and Perm.mul_apply) gives σ x = x · σ 1 for all x, so σ = rightReg (σ 1)⁻¹ lies in R(G). Reverse inclusion is pure associativity: left and right translations commute because (g'·x)·g⁻¹ = g'·(x·g⁻¹) (mul_assoc).
mathContext: $\sigma$ commutes with all $L(x)\Rightarrow \sigma x = x\,\sigma(1)\Rightarrow \sigma = R(\sigma(1)^{-1})$; and $C_{\operatorname{Sym}(G)}(L(G)) = R(G)$.

title: The mirror: centralizer of the right-regular image is the left-regular image
content: centralizer_rightReg_range is the symmetric statement: Subgroup.centralizer ↑(rightReg G).range = (leftReg G).range. The argument mirrors the previous theorem — a permutation commuting with every rightReg x⁻¹, evaluated at 1, satisfies σ x = σ 1 · x, identifying σ = leftReg (σ 1); the reverse inclusion is again associativity. Together the two theorems express the centralizer duality: each regular image is exactly the centralizer of the other inside Sym(G).
mathContext: $C_{\operatorname{Sym}(G)}(R(G)) = L(G)$; $\;\sigma$ commutes with all $R(x)\Rightarrow \sigma x = \sigma(1)\,x = L(\sigma(1))x$.

title: Equal images iff abelian; self-centralizing iff abelian
content: leftReg_range_eq_rightReg_range_iff proves (leftReg G).range = (rightReg G).range ↔ ∀ x y, x·y = y·x. Forward: equality writes leftReg x = rightReg z for some z; evaluating at 1 forces z = x⁻¹, and evaluating at a general y yields y·x = x·y. Reverse: if G is abelian then mulLeft g = mulRight g, so leftReg g = rightReg g⁻¹ and the ranges agree. leftReg_range_le_centralizer_iff then derives 'the left-regular image lies in its own centralizer iff G is abelian' by rewriting through centralizer_leftReg_range — recovering 'self-centralizing ⟺ commutative' directly from the centralizer identity.
mathContext: $L(G) = R(G) \iff \forall x,y,\; xy = yx$; and $L(G) \le C(L(G)) \iff G$ abelian.
